stories.headline: Update: Russia and Ukraine Agree to Large Prisoner Exchange as US Envoys Prepare to Meet Putin
stories.summary:
Russia and Ukraine agreed to a large exchange of prisoners of war, both sides said Wednesday, as two days of U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi ended without a major breakthrough on ending the nearly five-year-old full-scale invasion. The exchange was described as the largest humanitarian release since the war began in 2022.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who arrived in Ireland ahead of talks with U.S. envoys on Thursday, said there was a "window of opportunity" in which all participants genuinely want a result before 2027. He said he hoped Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner would bring back "specifics" from a planned meeting with Vladimir Putin in Moscow. The talks centered on a European security framework.

Axios reported that the United States has asked Russia to submit a new proposal for a future security agreement with Europe that includes Russian steps to ease tension with the continent. Moscow has long sought a deal limiting NATO expansion and scaling back military presence in Eastern Europe, demands Washington has previously rejected but now appears open to in some form as part of a broader settlement.

The diplomacy continues alongside military pressure. Ukraine and Russia have exchanged attacks on each other's capitals, and Putin appears intent on damaging Ukraine's economy ahead of what Kyiv expects to be its hardest winter yet. Some European commentators have warned that a deal giving Moscow territory and sanctions relief could come within weeks, while European leaders remain divided.

stories.headline: Update: Nvidia Board Reportedly Preparing to Oust CEO Jensen Huang After Second Affair Report
stories.summary:
Nvidia's board is preparing to remove CEO Jensen Huang, according to reports from the Wall Street Journal and other outlets, after the New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang had a second affair, this one with a senior executive who reports to him. Nvidia shares fell more than 8 percent in after-hours trading, dropping below $160 for the first time since June 2025.

The company is already investigating Huang over a relationship with Alice Huang, a woman U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly believe was a Chinese asset. Earlier this month Huang apologized to his company and family. The woman was reportedly associated with Megaspeed, a firm that bought nearly $5 billion in AI chips and hardware from Nvidia and denies wrongdoing.

The matter has become a national security and political issue. Axios reported that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over the failure to place Megaspeed on a national security concerns list, and that Lutnick had been sent a highly classified memo about Huang's relationship. Sen. Kevin Cramer, a Republican, said Huang should resign. Democratic Reps. Raja Krishnamoorthi and Suzan DelBene called for investigations, with Krishnamoorthi saying Huang should be subpoenaed if he declines a voluntary interview. President Trump has defended Huang, which critics say raises questions about his ties to industry leaders.

Huang leads what is arguably the world's most powerful technology company, whose chips underpin the AI boom, so a leadership change could affect competitors and broader markets.

stories.headline: White House Warns Democratic Oversight Plans 'May Cross the Line Into Blatant Criminality'
stories.summary:
White House counsel Will Scharf sent a letter Wednesday to Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, warning that Democratic promises to investigate the Trump administration "may cross the line into blatant criminality." The letter came as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January after winning the midterms.

Garcia responded that the Constitution gives Congress latitude to conduct investigations, and said the threat suggests Trump has "something to hide." House Democrats said they would not be intimidated. Rep. Suzan DelBene said Democrats will conduct oversight and require administration officials to appear before Congress, while also focusing on costs and health care.

The administration's position is that aggressive probes could be abusive or unlawful, while Democrats and many legal observers note that oversight is a standard congressional function. The warning comes amid reports of a wave of resignations within the Justice Department, and as Democrats separately plan scrutiny of matters including Nvidia and the Iran war.

The exchange foreshadows a confrontational two years. Republicans, meanwhile, are reorganizing after heavy midterm losses: House Republicans elected Jim Jordan as minority leader over Steve Scalise, and Senate Republicans agreed to a resolution to maximize their remaining 54 days in power. Democratic leaders have not said which probes will come first.

stories.headline: Update: Iran Warns of Strikes on US Bases Beyond Gulf; Israel Reportedly Orders Stepped-Up Attack Preparations
stories.summary:
Iran's top national security official warned that Tehran would strike American bases beyond the Gulf, including in Europe, if the United States resumes air strikes on Iran. The warning came a day after U.S. indictments of three men accused of Iranian-linked plots, including an attempt against a British air base housing U.S. aircraft. Israeli media separately reported that Israel's security cabinet ordered the military to step up preparations for a possible attack on Iran.

Iranian officials said any renewed offensive would bring "far more deadly blows." The Revolutionary Guard showcased an underground "missile city" and claimed three vessels caught fire after striking naval mines while taking an unauthorized route through the Strait of Hormuz, a claim not independently verified. Iran's Mohsen Rezaei urged Washington to accept Tehran's demands, including lifting sanctions and the blockade of its ports.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking in Paris, called the demands "absurd" and said Iran faces growing economic pressure and that no major military action was needed for now. Axios reported he told G7 counterparts that Trump weighed resuming the war or striking a deal but chose to strangle the Iranian regime economically. President Trump said at Arlington on Veterans Day that the conflict will end soon and promised "total victory."

The war has become a political burden for Republicans. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reportedly moved to a military base over an Iranian threat to his life, and Democrats and some Republicans continue to scrutinize the administration's conduct of the war.

stories.headline: Germany's Ruling Coalition Delays New Taxes and Rolls Back Welfare Cuts to Clear Way for 2027 Budget
stories.summary:
The parties in Chancellor Friedrich Merz's ruling coalition rolled back some planned social-spending cuts and delayed new taxes on Wednesday, clearing the way for a deal on Germany's 2027 budget. The agreement also delays a power-tax cut, according to Bloomberg's reporting.

The compromise reflects the balancing act within the coalition between fiscal discipline and protecting social programs. Rolling back welfare cuts softens measures that had drawn resistance, while postponing new taxes defers some revenue measures that had been under discussion.

The budget is significant because Germany is Europe's largest economy, and its fiscal choices affect growth and spending across the euro area. Commentary from the right, including National Review, argued that fiscal conservatives should pursue the same aim for all taxes: broaden the base and reduce the rate. Critics of the delays may argue that postponing revenue measures while reversing spending cuts leaves budget gaps unresolved, while supporters see the changes as necessary to maintain coalition unity.

stories.headline: Egyptian Journalist Lina Attalah's Retrial Adjourned as UN Warns of Assaults on Press Freedom
stories.summary:
A criminal court in Cairo on Wednesday postponed the retrial of prominent Egyptian journalist Lina Attalah until 18 November after her defence lawyers requested a new judge. Attalah is editor-in-chief of the independent news outlet Mada Masr. Her lawyers argued the judge had already formed a conviction against her.

Last month, a misdemeanours court convicted her of running a website without a licence, fining her 3 million Egyptian pounds (about $56,000) and ordering Mada Masr shut down. She then learned a court had in 2024 sentenced her in absentia to one year in prison for spreading false news and operating an unlicensed website. She is now being retried in that case by the same judge, and her appeal of last month's conviction is scheduled for 25 November.

The UN has warned of widening assaults on press freedom by Egyptian authorities, including the targeting and harassment of independent journalists. Attalah told the BBC the crackdown was meant to send a chilling message to the few remaining newsrooms. Egypt ranks 169th of 180 countries in Reporters Without Borders' 2026 index, with at least 26 journalists held in detention.

stories.headline: Four Grizzly Bears Killed in British Columbia After Fatal Attack on Mother and Daughter
stories.summary:
Four grizzly bears have been killed in connection with a fatal attack on a mother and daughter in Bella Coola, British Columbia. Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, died earlier this month after going for an afternoon walk in a trail area. Forensic testing and DNA analysis conclusively linked a sow and her three cubs to the attack.

The BC Conservation Officer Service destroyed all four animals in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict guidelines. Inspector Jeff Tyre said on Tuesday that the attack likely involved predatory behaviour, which he described as very rare. More than a dozen officers took part in the investigation amid difficult terrain and weather.

DNA testing also confirmed the bears were not involved in a November 2025 attack on a school group in the same area, in which 11 people were injured and the responsible bear was never found. Nuxalk Nation Chief Samuel Schooner said the latest attack was deeply re-triggering for the community as it recovers from last year's incident. Balcarras's brother described the two women as two peas in a pod.

stories.headline: Russia's Ambassador to the US Alexander Darchiev Dies Suddenly at 66
stories.summary:
Russia's Foreign Ministry announced on Wednesday that its ambassador to the United States, Alexander Darchiev, died suddenly on November 11 at the age of 66. A statement shared on the government's Telegram channel did not give a cause of death. The ministry expressed "profound sorrow" at the loss of the veteran diplomat.

Darchiev had been appointed by President Vladimir Putin to lead a rapprochement with the Trump administration. His death comes while Russia, Ukraine and the United States are engaged in talks in Abu Dhabi, which U.S. officials have described as productive.

No further details were released about the circumstances of his death. It is not yet clear who will succeed him in Washington or how the vacancy might affect the diplomatic channel between Moscow and the Trump administration. Further information from Russian authorities is expected in the coming days.

stories.headline: Which Key Races Remain Undecided One Week After the US Midterms
stories.summary:
More than a week after the midterm elections, the final size of the Democratic majorities in both chambers of Congress remains undetermined. Democrats have won 54 Senate seats for the incoming Congress and hold 255 House seats, their largest elected House majority since 2008. More than a dozen congressional races are still uncalled.

In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola led Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by about 2,500 votes with an estimated 76 percent counted. She is just over one percentage point short of an outright majority, so the race could go to ranked-choice tabulation on November 18. The final overseas absentee ballots are accepted through that date, and the state's target for certification is November 25.

In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom led Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith by roughly 2,500 to 2,600 votes, in a state Donald Trump carried by more than 22 points in 2024. Officials estimated 12,000 to 20,000 affidavit ballots were cast, and about 15,500 had been processed as of Tuesday morning. Mississippi has no automatic recounts, and both parties have sent legal teams. Counties must submit results by Friday, with state certification set for December 3. A Colom win would make him the state's first Democratic senator in nearly four decades and its first Black senator in over 140 years.

stories.headline: Missing 11-Month-Old Found Buried Alive in Crate in South Carolina
stories.summary:
An 11-month-old boy, Koah Sharpe, was rescued in South Carolina after officials said his father buried him alive in a crate. The child had been missing since Monday, when his father, Michael Comer, 25, took him from his mother's house. Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said the baby was found Tuesday, apparently after about 24 hours underground.

Comer was arrested Monday evening on a burglary charge without the child, and he told investigators little about the boy's whereabouts. A search party of about 100 police and fire personnel searched woods near his home and noticed freshly disturbed dirt. As they dug, they heard a baby crying, which Koon called "the most joyful sound you ever heard."

The boy was in a roughly two-foot dog crate wrapped in a towel, which the sheriff said probably gave enough air, while cold weather kept him from overheating. He is in hospital and Koon said he was hopeful of a full recovery. Authorities are deciding on further charges, and court records show Comer previously pleaded guilty to domestic violence charges.

stories.headline: Indonesia's Vice President Gibran Resigns Amid Signs Ruling Alliance Is Fraying
stories.summary:
Indonesia's Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has submitted his resignation, an aide told the BBC. The aide, Budi Arie, said the letter was delivered directly to President Prabowo Subianto on Wednesday. It remains unclear whether Prabowo has accepted it.

The resignation follows a ruling by Indonesia's Supreme Court that a high-school document Gibran used in his 2024 campaign was invalid. The court said there was no evidence he had a foreign diploma or certificate that could serve as the basis for equivalency with a senior high school qualification. It cited an earlier Constitutional Court ruling from October that reached the same conclusion. More than 100 lawmakers then backed a parliamentary initiative that could have opened the way to impeachment proceedings. On Tuesday, Gibran had asked for the chance to challenge the ruling and prove his credentials, according to State Secretary Prasetyo Hadi.

Gibran, the son of outgoing president Joko Widodo, known as Jokowi, joined Prabowo's ticket as part of an alliance between Jokowi and his former rival. He was 36 at the time and became eligible only after a controversial Constitutional Court ruling exempted him from the minimum age of 40. Tensions between Jokowi and Prabowo appear to have grown, with Prabowo sidelining Jokowi's Nusantara capital project and reshuffling Jokowi loyalists, including finance minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati. Last week, presidential chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo, a Jokowi ally, was arrested on suspicion of wiretapping the president and sacked a day later.

stories.headline: Bomb Threat Emails Hit Thousands of Schools in Italy, Scotland and Northern Ireland
stories.summary:
About 6,300 schools across Italy and more than 700 in Scotland and Northern Ireland received bomb threats on Wednesday, according to local authorities. Some buildings in Italy were evacuated as a precaution, but Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said checks had shown no evidence of concrete danger. She said the reports appeared linked to a strategy intended to cause alarm.

Italian officials said a single email appeared to have been sent to 6,300 of the country's 7,476 state schools. It was signed by a purported "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan". Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara said the incidents were probably a cyber-attack rather than a genuine risk. One Milan headteacher said the sender's address had already been flagged as spam by a university student in Taiwan.

In Scotland, police said the warnings were immediately assessed as hoaxes and advised that schools did not need to evacuate based solely on the emails, though some local authorities did evacuate some schools. Education secretary Mairi McAllan said specialist cyber-crime officers were working to identify the source. Northern Ireland officials told schools to stay open unless police advised otherwise. It is unclear whether the incidents are connected, but officials noted they follow bomb hoaxes last week that disrupted Italian airports and airlines elsewhere in Europe, as well as threats against supermarkets and hospitals. An extremist misogynistic group claimed some earlier threats but later denied any link.

stories.headline: Chilean Transport Workers Block Highways Over Surging Diesel Prices
stories.summary:
Hundreds of bus and lorry drivers in Chile began blocking roads and highways nationwide on Tuesday to protest high fuel prices. They gathered in convoys to halt traffic along major routes. The protesters are demanding relief from diesel costs driven up by the war in Iran.

Talks between government officials and protest leaders have failed to produce a resolution, and another meeting is expected Wednesday. The protest is organized by the Fuerza del Norte trade union, which represents about 80% of Chile's lorry drivers, and the No+TAG civic movement. No+TAG spokesman Andres Alarcon said there was no point of agreement with the government and the strike continues.

Economy Minister Daniel Mas called for further dialogue but warned that at some point the highways would have to be cleared, saying the protests were hurting economic activity and exports. Industry groups say average diesel prices have risen 74% since March, and President Jose Antonio Kast's government has faced public discontent over fuel costs for months. The head of an intercity bus owners' association said operators had reached their limit after more than a month of losses.

stories.headline: CDC Chief Says Measles Response Unchanged if U.S. Loses Elimination Status
stories.summary:
The head of the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said the agency's response to ongoing measles outbreaks would not change if the country loses its measles elimination status this month. "Let's say we did lose our measles elimination status. We're going to be doing the same exact thing that we've been doing today," the official said, describing continued outbreak response work.

The United States could lose the status after measles cases more than doubled over the past year. Elimination status generally depends on the absence of continuous disease transmission over a sustained period, and losing it would be a symbolic and public health setback for a disease once declared eliminated domestically.

Public health experts, including CBS News contributor Dr. Celine Gounder, have weighed in on the implications. The statement signals the agency does not plan new measures tied to the formal designation, and the decision on the country's status is expected later this month.

stories.headline: Update: House Republicans Block Effort to Impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
stories.summary:
The House voted Tuesday evening to turn aside a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, ending for now an effort to remove him over his conduct in office and his handling of the war in Iran. The vote followed Hegseth's first news conference in six months, in which he called the effort a farce. The resolution, pushed by Rep. Thomas Massie, focused on Hegseth's involvement in some of the most controversial episodes of President Trump's second term.

Axios reported that the outcome is a victory for Hegseth, the Trump administration and Republican leaders, who had been bracing for a possible rebellion within their own ranks. Some House Republicans had warned in recent days that the measure could pass. Supporters of Hegseth have defended his leadership of the Pentagon and dismissed the impeachment push as politically motivated, while critics say his conduct warrants a formal rebuke.

The reprieve is likely to be short-lived. Democrats, who won back the House majority in the midterm elections, are widely expected to force the issue again once they take control in January. The vote came as Republicans reshuffled their own leadership, with the House GOP choosing Jim Jordan as its new leader and Senate Republicans re-electing John Thune amid calls from some members to delay the vote.

stories.headline: Spain Hit by First General Strike in 14 Years Over Housing and Cost of Living
stories.summary:
Transport and other public services across Spain faced serious disruption Wednesday in the country's first general strike since 2012, called by the main unions over housing and the high cost of living. Traffic was halted on several main roads in Madrid and Catalonia, and large demonstrations were planned for Madrid and Barcelona later in the day. The interior ministry said dozens of people were arrested for various incidents, and Spanish reports said estate agencies had been attacked.

Union leaders described the turnout differently from business groups. UGT head Pepe Alvarez called participation massive, and CC OO's Unai Sordo called it very significant, while the Spanish Confederation of Business Organisations said participation was low and uneven by area and sector. The strike was triggered by protests over affordable housing after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from her Madrid flat of seven decades; she died weeks later. A 50-square-meter Madrid apartment averaged EUR 1,170 a month in October, nearly half the average gross monthly salary of about EUR 2,460.

The strike is politically unusual because Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez and his ministers encouraged workers to take part. Sanchez called snap elections for November 29 after parliament failed to approve his housing reform plan. The opposition People's Party, leading in the polls, accused the government of weaponizing the strike for electoral gain, and leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo called it nonsense and denounced the unions.

stories.headline: Colom Extends Slim Lead Over Hyde-Smith in Mississippi Senate Race as Ballot Deadlines Near
stories.summary:
Democrat Scott Colom has extended his narrow lead over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's Senate race by more than 3,000 votes, according to The Hill's election partner Decision Desk HQ. With around 95 percent of ballots counted, the race remains unresolved a week after Democrats posted sweeping midterm victories nationwide.

Mississippi, a state not known for close contests, is now at the center of national attention. An unusually high number of absentee and provisional ballots remain to be tallied ahead of two crucial ballot deadlines, and those votes will help determine the size of the Democratic majority in the Senate.

PBS NewsHour reported on how election officials are handling the ongoing count, calling the race historic. The outcome could widen Democratic control of the chamber and carries added weight as Republicans manage leadership turmoil and a difficult lame-duck session following their midterm losses.

stories.headline: Kenya Discharges Last Ebola Patient, Begins 42-Day Countdown to Virus-Free Status
stories.summary:
Kenya has discharged its last Ebola patient, the seventh to recover, and now begins a 42-day countdown to being declared Ebola-free. The country confirmed its first-ever case in early October, when a Kenyan businessman who had contracted the virus in the Democratic Republic of Congo died within days of arriving in Nairobi. His mother also died. Four of the recovered patients were healthcare workers.

Health Minister Aden Duale said all 135 identified contacts had completed 21 days in isolation, and no new confirmed cases have been reported since October 20. Officials found no evidence of wider community transmission. Under World Health Organization guidelines, 42 days must pass after the last patient tests negative and is discharged before an outbreak can be declared over.

The outbreak in DR Congo, which began in May, has killed more than 5,000 people. Kenya will maintain heightened surveillance at borders, airports and health facilities, and returning travelers must complete health declarations, be screened and quarantine for 21 days. Duale urged countries that imposed travel and visa restrictions to reconsider them. Africa CDC chief Jean Kaseya called the milestone encouraging but urged continued vigilance.

stories.headline: Update: Eisenkot Tasked With Forming Israeli Government, Unveils Agenda to Reverse Netanyahu Policies
stories.summary:
Gadi Eisenkot, the main political rival of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, has been given the first opportunity to build a new Israeli government. He has pledged to reverse many of Netanyahu's policies. The new Knesset was sworn in on the day the agenda was announced.

Newly elected lawmakers opposed to Netanyahu unveiled a series of bills targeting the prime minister on the opening day. The move signals that his rivals are eager to undo his political legacy following their recent election victory.

The path to a governing coalition remains uncertain. BBC reporting on the vote count, with more than 90 percent of ballots tallied, said all signs pointed to an impasse, with new elections a possible outcome. Analysts have also pointed to the ultra-Orthodox community's resistance to being drafted into the Israeli army as a factor that could affect the stability of any coalition, including Netanyahu's.

The political shift comes amid regional tension, including the Gaza humanitarian situation after heavy flooding and an ongoing conflict involving Iran. Eisenkot now faces the task of assembling a majority in a fragmented parliament.

stories.headline: Stephen Miller, New Chief of Staff, Aims to Win Back Young and Minority Men After Midterms
stories.summary:
Stephen Miller plans to use his new role as White House chief of staff to win back young and minority men who helped elect President Trump in 2024 but swung toward Democrats in the midterms, according to two people familiar with the administration's plans who spoke to Axios. Miller was named last week to replace Susie Wiles.

He intends to revive the populist agenda that helped build the president's 2024 coalition, with an emphasis on working-class voters. Miller is widely known as the architect of the administration's tough immigration policies.

Supporters of the appointment view it as a commitment to the core agenda that won Trump the presidency. Critics, including some Democrats, see it as a sign the president does not intend to pursue the bipartisan tone he suggested after the election. One possible 2028 Democratic contender told Politico that Democrats should try to work with Miller despite a "well of distrust."

The shake-up comes as Republicans face a difficult lame-duck session and a looming shutdown deadline after their midterm losses.

stories.headline: El Salvador Says Military Destroyed Headquarters of Haitian 400 Mawozo Gang
stories.summary:
El Salvador's military has destroyed the headquarters of 400 Mawozo, one of Haiti's largest gangs, President Nayib Bukele said. The ground and air attack targeted a complex on the outskirts of Port-au-Prince, reportedly in Croix-des-Bouquets. It is the first Salvadoran military action on a Haitian target since more than 2,000 soldiers deployed last month.

The deployment followed the abduction in October of four Salvadoran air force technicians working with the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force. Bukele has vowed to bring them home alive. Some media outlets reported as many as 20 people were killed, though authorities have not confirmed that, and the BBC could not verify Bukele's video. The Miami Herald reported the gang leader, Wilson Joseph, was not present.

Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aime thanked El Salvador and said the two nations would keep working together to restore state authority. Critics, including Amnesty International, have raised concerns about the operational legitimacy and legality of the Salvadoran troops' actions, saying they are not all operating within the Gang Suppression Force command structure.

stories.headline: Update: Chicago Fed's Goolsbee Calls October Inflation Report 'Borderline Disturbing'
stories.summary:
Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee described the latest consumer price report as "distressing, borderline disturbing." Prices rose 0.4 percent in October, driven largely by food and energy, while housing costs climbed 0.3 percent and accounted for roughly a third of the larger-than-expected increase. Economists now expect inflation of about 4 percent for the year, outpacing wage growth.

Goolsbee said the effects of tariffs on goods prices were supposed to have faded by now but continue. He called services inflation, including health care, the most troubling element, saying it is probably not mainly driven by oil prices or tariffs and is not transitory. He noted energy costs are elevated because of the war in the Middle East, and that demand tied to the AI build-out is now adding pressure.

The comments come as markets weigh a possible Fed rate hike, after Governor Christopher Waller floated a half-point increase. Goolsbee said the Fed has a limited toolset, only the interest rate, and that inflation is on the minds of businesses, nonprofits and consumers across the Midwest, including farmers hit by diesel costs.
